I · Theory

One encoder proposes a distribution for each input

Rather than optimise a new guess from scratch, learn a reusable function.

x ⟶ qφ(z∣x)x\ \longrightarrow\ q_\varphi(z\mid x)x ⟶ qφ​(z∣x)
Soφ\varphiφ are shared parameters; the output is a distribution, not one hidden answer.NextWhat can train this function when exact posteriors are unavailable?

Keep the model fixed. Each term below answers a different question.

ExpressionMeaning

I · Theory

A computable score trains the posterior guesses

For each proposed hidden value, compare the model and encoder probabilities.

L(φ;x)=Ez∼qφ[log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qφ(z∣x)⏟one full sample training term]\mathcal L(\varphi;x)=\mathbb E_{z\sim q_\varphi}[\underbrace{\log p(x,z)-\log q_\varphi(z\mid x)}_{\text{one full sample training term}}]L(φ;x)=Ez∼qφ​​[one full sample training termlogp(x,z)−logqφ​(z∣x)​​]

Assume the generative model is already given: p(z)p(z)p(z) and p(x∣z)p(x\mid z)p(x∣z) are known and fixed. Observe xxx, then let the encoder propose zzz. Evaluate p(x,z)=p(z)p(x∣z)p(x,z)=p(z)p(x\mid z)p(x,z)=p(z)p(x∣z) to score that proposal. Here we train only the encoder.

Why computable? Draw zzz from the encoder; evaluate the known p(x,z)p(x,z)p(x,z) and qφ(z∣x)q_\varphi(z\mid x)qφ​(z∣x); average the scores. No true posterior needed. Sampling estimates the expectation.

SoRaise the average score by changing the encoder, without posterior labels.NextWhy should a higher score improve the guess?
I · Theory

The score is evidence minus posterior error

Hold the generative model fixed while comparing encoder guesses.

log⁡p(x)=L(φ;x)+KL(qφ∥p(z∣x))⏟nonnegative posterior gap\log p(x)=\mathcal L(\varphi;x)+\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(q_\varphi\|p(z\mid x))}_{\text{nonnegative posterior gap}}logp(x)=L(φ;x)+nonnegative posterior gapKL(qφ​∥p(z∣x))​​

I · Theory

All observations update the same encoder

Each observation contributes its own lower bound.

training objective=∑kL(φ;xk)\text{training objective}=\sum_k\mathcal L(\varphi;x_k)training objective=∑k​L(φ;xk​)

I · Theory

Two restrictions leave a posterior KL gap

First ask what each best separate guess can express; then impose a shared function.

RestrictionName of the resulting loss
Allowed distributions cannot match a posteriorApproximation gap
Shared encoder cannot reach the best separate guessesAmortization gap
SoIncomplete optimisation can add further loss beyond these best attainable gaps.NextIf log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qφ(z∣x)\log p(x,z)-\log q_\varphi(z\mid x)logp(x,z)−logqφ​(z∣x) contains a difficult expectation, how do we evaluate it?
Classroom checkpoint · Predict, explain, then reveal

Can longer training repair a missing input?

Discuss with a neighbour for one minute. Give a reason, not only an answer.

Two different observations become the same encoder input. Can more training produce two different outputs?
Answer. No. The same deterministic encoder input gives the same output; restore the missing information.
SoIdentify the restriction before changing the optimiser.NextIf the expected score is hard to compute, how can samples estimate it?
I · Theory

Average sampled scores when the integral is hard

Draw possible hidden values from the encoder and score them using the same rule.

OperationMeaning
DrawGenerate candidates from the current guess
ScoreCompute model log probability minus encoder log probability
AverageEstimate the expected score
SoSampling approximates the lower bound L\mathcal LL; it does not reveal the true hidden value.NextHow do the sampled scores tell us which parameters to change?
I · Theory

Gradients tell the encoder which way to change

We want the sampling rule to generate candidates with higher average training scores.

At the current parametersSmall gradient-ascent update
Positive derivativeIncrease that parameter
Negative derivativeDecrease that parameter
SoImprove the distribution’s expected score, rather than guaranteeing every draw improves.NextHow do we differentiate a score whose samples also depend on the encoder?
I · Theory · Make sampling easy to differentiate

Build a random sample in two simple steps

The encoder chooses where the guess is centred and how spread out it is.

StepAction
1 · Draw a random offsetDraw ε\varepsilonε from the fixed standard normal N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1)
2 · Place the candidateMultiply by the encoder's spread sss, then add its centre μ\muμ
z⏟candidate=μ⏟centre+s⏟standard deviation⋅ε⏟random offset\underbrace{z}_{\text{candidate}}=\underbrace{\mu}_{\text{centre}}+\underbrace{s}_{\text{standard deviation}}\cdot\underbrace{\varepsilon}_{\text{random offset}}candidatez​​=centreμ​​+standard deviations​​⋅random offsetε​​

To calculate one gradient, keep that offset fixed and track how changing the encoder moves the candidate. Draw fresh offsets for subsequent estimates.

SoThe encoder controls centre and spread; randomness comes from a separate, unchanged noise distribution.NextWhy can these random gradient estimates be useful on average?
I · Theory

A correct average can still yield noisy updates

Under regularity conditions, sampled gradients average to the true gradient.

What followsWhat does not follow
The estimator is unbiasedEvery step improves the objective
Averaging can reduce sampling noiseTraining reaches a global optimum
SoConvergence needs additional conditions; unbiasedness alone is insufficient.NextCan even an optimised encoder leave the hidden variable unused?
Classroom checkpoint · Predict, explain, then reveal

What is the encoder actually being trained to do?

Take one minute to explain the goal without using the word “gradient”.

Which objective have we defined?
Answer. Raise the expected log joint minus encoder log density; this targets a distribution, not one best hidden value.
SoTraining improves an expected score; individual random draws can be worse.NextWhat happens if the decoder does not need the hidden variable?
I · Theory

A hidden variable can become unnecessary

Read the same bound as fit to the observation minus departure from the prior.

L=Eqlog⁡p(x∣z)⏟fit−KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))⏟prior penalty\mathcal L=\underbrace{\mathbb E_q\log p(x\mid z)}_{\text{fit}}-\underbrace{\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))}_{\text{prior penalty}}L=fitEq​logp(x∣z)​​−prior penaltyKL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))​​

Fit: do the proposed hidden values make the observed xxx likely?
Prior penalty: how far does the whole guessed distribution q(z∣x)q(z\mid x)q(z∣x) move from our original assumption p(z)p(z)p(z)? It is zero when they match.

SoIf the decoder gives the same observation probabilities for every z, changing the encoder cannot change fit. Choosing q = prior then removes the prior penalty KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z)). This is a condition, not a consequence of network size.NextWhat changes when the generative model also learns?
I · Theory

Learning the model adds a decoder to the story

The encoder learns hidden-value guesses; the decoder learns how hidden values explain observations.

ParametersRole
Encoder φ\varphiφProposes a distribution from an observation
Decoder θ\thetaθSpecifies observation probabilities from a hidden value
Sothe lower bound L\mathcal LL can rise because the encoder reduces its posterior error, even if the changing model gives the data lower likelihood.NextHow does learning the encoder and decoder relate to the E-step and M-step?
I · Connection to expectation–maximization

The same lower bound connects EM and the encoder

Recall L(θ,q;x)=Eq[log⁡pθ(x,z)−log⁡q(z)]\mathcal L(\theta,q;x)=\mathbb E_q[\log p_\theta(x,z)-\log q(z)]L(θ,q;x)=Eq​[logpθ​(x,z)−logq(z)]. θ\thetaθ controls the model; qqq guesses the hidden variable.

MethodInfer the hidden variableLearn the model
Exact EM · Lecture 5E-step: set each qqq to its exact posteriorM-step: maximise the bound in θ\thetaθ
Variational EM · Lecture 6Optimise each qqq within an allowed familyImprove the same bound in θ\thetaθ
Amortized inference · TodayOne shared qφ(z∣x)q_\varphi(z\mid x)qφ​(z∣x) supplies the guessesWhen learned, update decoder θ\thetaθ too

Different guarantees: exact EM's E-step makes the bound tight before its M-step. A shared approximate encoder need not do so; joint gradient updates do not inherit EM's monotonic likelihood guarantee.

SoThe encoder shares the work of the E-step; it is not automatically an exact E-step.NextWhat exact E-step calculation does an encoder replace in our Gaussian example?

The encoder replaces per-observation posterior solving

Keep z∼N(0,1)z\sim N(0,1)z∼N(0,1), x=z+ηx=z+\etax=z+η, η∼N(0,1)\eta\sim N(0,1)η∼N(0,1), and observed x=1.6x=1.6x=1.6. Hold the model fixed.

Exact EM E-stepTrained encoder
Compute p(z∣x)=N(x/2,1/2)p(z\mid x)=N(x/2,1/2)p(z∣x)=N(x/2,1/2)Evaluate qφ(z∣x)=N(ax,s2)q_\varphi(z\mid x)=N(ax,s^2)qφ​(z∣x)=N(ax,s2)
For this observation: N(0.8,0.5)N(0.8,0.5)N(0.8,0.5)Learned a=0.5,s2=0.5a=0.5,s^2=0.5a=0.5,s2=0.5: output N(0.8,0.5)N(0.8,0.5)N(0.8,0.5)
Repeat posterior inference for each observationReuse the same learned mapping on each observation

Why faster in difficult models? Replace many inference iterations per observation with one network evaluation. Pay for training beforehand. This Gaussian E-step already has a cheap formula, so it does not demonstrate a speedup.

SoThe encoder replaces how the E-step's posterior guess is obtained, not the model update. If the model changes, the encoder may need updating too.NextHow are these components used for reconstruction and fresh generation?

Training uses the encoder; generation starts from the prior

The encoder explains existing observations. The generative model can also create new ones.

TaskRoute
Reconstruct an observationGiven xxx → draw z∼qφ(z∣x)z\sim q_\varphi(z\mid x)z∼qφ​(z∣x) → decode
Generate a new observationDraw z∼p(z)z\sim p(z)z∼p(z) → draw x∼pθ(x∣z)x\sim p_\theta(x\mid z)x∼pθ​(x∣z)
Train on dataEncode → sample → score → update both networks

The observation shifts our guess toward its value

Combine the chosen prior with the information from one noisy observation.

Our chosen model: z∼N(0,1)z\sim N(0,1)z∼N(0,1); x=z+ηx=z+\etax=z+η, with independent noise η∼N(0,1)\eta\sim N(0,1)η∼N(0,1). Here N(mean,variance)N(\text{mean},\text{variance})N(mean,variance).

Multiply the two curves, then complete one square

The green curve comes from multiplying the prior and likelihood.

p(z∣x)∝e−z2/2⋅e−(x−z)2/2=e−{z2+(x−z)2}/2p(z\mid x)\propto e^{-z^2/2}\cdot e^{-(x-z)^2/2}=e^{-\{z^2+(x-z)^2\}/2}p(z∣x)∝e−z2/2⋅e−(x−z)2/2=e−{z2+(x−z)2}/2

Read the bell. The term x2/2x^2/2x2/2 is constant in zzz, so normalization absorbs it:
p(z∣x)∝e−(z−x/2)2=e−(z−μ)2/(2v)p(z\mid x)\propto e^{-(z-x/2)^2}=e^{-(z-\mu)^2/(2v)}p(z∣x)∝e−(z−x/2)2=e−(z−μ)2/(2v). Thus μ=x/2\mu=x/2μ=x/2, v=1/2v=1/2v=1/2.
For our observation. Mean: 1.6/2=0.81.6/2=\mathbf{0.8}1.6/2=0.8. Variance: 0.5\mathbf{0.5}0.5. Equal prior and noise variances give an equal-weight mean; two clues reduce uncertainty.

One complete training loop ties the pieces together

StepAction

The hidden representation can make generation cheaper

Transfer the idea from hidden variable choices to hidden image representations.

SoAn encoder and decoder connect pixels to a smaller latent space.NextCount the entries in one specific image and latent representation.
III · Applications

Count the image entries before comparing costs

Count the entries in one specific image and latent representation.

SoThis design reduces the number of entries by a factor of 48.NextA smaller grid changes the number of positions an attention layer compares.
III · Applications

Attention compares each position with every position

A position is one grid cell. In full attention, each cell compares itself with all cells, including itself.

Small illustrationPositions NFull-attention comparisons N × N
4 × 4 grid1616 × 16 = 256
2 × 2 grid44 × 4 = 16
SoFour times fewer positions gives 16 times fewer pair comparisons. This counts attention pairs, not total generation speed.NextWhat information must the encoder retain so the decoder can rebuild an image?
III · Applications

Keep image details while regularising the hidden code

An image encoder produces a smaller hidden code. Its decoder must use that code to rebuild the original image's details.

Training requirementIn plain words
Reconstruction qualityKeep enough image information for the decoder
Prior penalty KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))Keep each guessed code distribution near the prior
Weight the two requirementsDecide how strongly to regularise while preserving useful details
A simplified weighted objective: reconstruction reward−β KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))\text{reconstruction reward}-\beta\,\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))reconstruction reward−βKL(q(z∣x)∥p(z)). Here β\betaβ sets the penalty weight.

If every image produced the same code distribution, the code would not distinguish their details. A weaker penalty may help retain information; it is not a guarantee. Image systems can also use perceptual and adversarial losses.

SoImage autoencoders balance useful reconstruction and latent regularisation. A modified loss need not be the original lower bound L\mathcal LL.NextWhere else do we reuse a learned function to infer hidden information?
III · Applications

The reusable idea is a learned inference function

The same hidden-value inference task also appears when experiments can be simulated.

SoA learned posterior proposal still needs calibration and distribution checks.NextReview each obstacle and the tool introduced to answer it.

The whole method starts with a hidden cause

We start withWe doWe check

A fitted encoderReuse on new casesAre its guesses accurate and informative?
SoUseful inference needs adequate inputs, expressive guesses and a trainable objective.NextTest the distinctions that determine when the shortcut helps or fails.
Check yourself

What prevents the encoder from matching Bayes?

Test the distinctions that determine when the shortcut helps or fails.

1. An encoder reads hhh and nnn and still has a gap. What has gone wrong?
Answer. The family or the training: with both inputs the posterior map is reachable , so a gap now means the family is too small or the fit is not at its best.
SoExplain a restriction's cause before choosing a remedy.NextWhy can training remain noisy even with a correct average gradient?
Check yourself

Why can a correct gradient still be noisy?

A sampled gradient can fluctuate even when its average is correct.

2. Why can log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qφ(z∣x)\log p(x,z)-\log q_\varphi(z\mid x)logp(x,z)−logqφ​(z∣x)-function gradient become noisy?
Answer. It judges every coordinate by one score for the whole draw, so the noise of that score enters every coordinate ; it stays correct on average.
SoAn unbiased estimate can still have high variance.NextDoes a zero prior penalty mean the posterior guess is exact?
Check yourself

Does a zero prior penalty mean a tight bound?

Prior penalty KL(q∥p(z))\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(z))KL(q∥p(z)) is different from posterior error KL(q∥p(z∣x))\mathrm{KL}(q\|p(z\mid x))KL(q∥p(z∣x)).

If KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))=0\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))=0KL(q(z∣x)∥p(z))=0 for every input, what does that tell us?
Choose “possibly uninformative: check the model”. Zero prior penalty means q(z∣x)=p(z)q(z\mid x)=p(z)q(z∣x)=p(z). Original model x=z+ηx=z+\etax=z+η, with x=1.6x=1.6x=1.6: the posterior is N(0.8,0.5)N(0.8,0.5)N(0.8,0.5), so returning prior N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) is incorrect. In the explicitly independent comparison model, p(z∣x)=p(z)=N(0,1)p(z\mid x)=p(z)=N(0,1)p(z∣x)=p(z)=N(0,1), so returning that prior is exact for that model.
SoZero prior penalty means q=p(z)q=p(z)q=p(z); it does not by itself mean q=p(z∣x)q=p(z\mid x)q=p(z∣x).NextThe continuous example inferred a clean hidden value behind noise.
9 · Example and mechanism

Diffusion removes noise over several learned steps

Generation starts from random latent noise. A trained denoiser repeatedly updates it; the decoder then maps the result to pixels.

SoThe denoiser generates a latent representation through repeated updates; the decoder turns the final representation into an image.NextNext lecture: how is this denoiser trained, and what does each reverse step predict?

Appendix · Part 1 · The measurement

Six steps per record, when the hidden part is a number

The claim of , measured on the model of Part 5 : a hidden number z∼N(0,1)z\sim N(0,1)z∼N(0,1) and a record x=z+noisex=z+\text{noise}x=z+noise. Four records, each climbing the lower bound L\mathcal LL from the prior.

Each record repeats the whole climb, and learns nothing from the records before it.

Calculation ·

One head means different things in different bags

Coin A favours heads. One head and three tails therefore argues against A more strongly than one head and one tail.
For two tosses, the A and B joint probabilities are 0.16,0.240.16,0.240.16,0.24, so the posterior is 0.16/(0.16+0.24)=0.400.16/(0.16+0.24)=0.400.16/(0.16+0.24)=0.40.
For four tosses, there are four positions for the single head. Multiplying prior, positions and toss probabilities gives 0.5⋅4⋅0.8⋅0.23=0.01280.5\cdot4\cdot0.8\cdot0.2^3=0.01280.5⋅4⋅0.8⋅0.23=0.0128 and 0.5⋅4⋅0.4⋅0.63=0.17280.5\cdot4\cdot0.4\cdot0.6^3=0.17280.5⋅4⋅0.4⋅0.63=0.1728. Thus A has probability 0.0128/0.1856≈0.0690.0128/0.1856\approx0.0690.0128/0.1856≈0.069.
Calculation ·

Reading both counts removes this input conflict

Give the encoder both hhh, the heads, and nnn, the tosses. The two bags now have different inputs.
The exact posterior can be written q(A∣h,n)=σ(hlog⁡6+nlog⁡(1/3))q(A\mid h,n)=\sigma(h\log6+n\log(1/3))q(A∣h,n)=σ(hlog6+nlog(1/3)), where σ(t)=1/(1+e−t)\sigma(t)=1/(1+e^{-t})σ(t)=1/(1+e−t). A head multiplies the A/B odds by 0.8/0.4=20.8/0.4=20.8/0.4=2; a tail multiplies them by 0.2/0.6=1/30.2/0.6=1/30.2/0.6=1/3.
A shared encoder with this form can fit every bag exactly. Complete inputs make this possible; successful training is still needed.
Calculation ·

More capacity helps only after inputs are sufficient

A larger network still cannot distinguish two bags if both arrive as the same input.
After including heads and tosses, a sufficiently expressive network can approximate the posterior map on a bounded input set.
For finite coins, continuity and probabilities bounded away from zero allow a small probability error to imply a small KL gap. This is an existence result, not a training guarantee.
Calculation ·

The observation shifts our guess toward its value

The prior favours a hidden value near zero. The noisy observation favours a hidden value near the observed number.
With equal noise variances, the posterior mean lies halfway: for x=2x=2x=2, the mean is 111.
Completing the square gives p(z∣x)=N(x/2,1/2)p(z\mid x)=N(x/2,1/2)p(z∣x)=N(x/2,1/2). Here 1/21/21/2 is the variance; the standard deviation is 1/2\sqrt{1/2}1/2​, not half the original width.
Calculation ·

Keep the noise fixed while changing the sample

Let the encoder choose mean μ\muμ and standard deviation sss. Draw independent standard-normal noise ε\varepsilonε.
Compute z=μ+s⋅εz=\mu+s\cdot\varepsilonz=μ+s⋅ε. For μ=1,s=2,ε=0.5\mu=1,s=2,\varepsilon=0.5μ=1,s=2,ε=0.5, the sample is 1+2⋅0.5=21+2\cdot0.5=21+2⋅0.5=2.
With that noise held fixed, changing μ\muμ moves the sample smoothly. The chain rule can now differentiate through zzz. This exact construction is for continuous Gaussian samples, not coin identities.
Calculation ·

Unbiased gradients need not reach the best solution

One sampled update can point downhill, just as one coin toss need not match its long-run frequency.
Under conditions permitting differentiation inside the expectation, the average estimated gradient equals the true gradient. See the appendix proof.
Convergence needs additional assumptions on smoothness, noise, stability and step sizes. Unbiasedness alone guarantees neither convergence nor a global optimum.
Calculation ·

Identical coins cannot be distinguished by tosses

Choose A or B equally often. Give both coins head probability 0.60.60.6. Observe one head in two tosses.
Each likelihood is 2⋅0.6⋅0.4=0.482\cdot0.6\cdot0.4=0.482⋅0.6⋅0.4=0.48. Each joint probability is 0.5⋅0.48=0.240.5\cdot0.48=0.240.5⋅0.48=0.24.
Bayes gives p(A∣x)=0.24/(0.24+0.24)=0.5p(A\mid x)=0.24/(0.24+0.24)=0.5p(A∣x)=0.24/(0.24+0.24)=0.5. The observation leaves our original equal probabilities unchanged.
Calculation ·

The lower bound identifies better encoder parameters

Keep the same observed value x=1.6x=1.6x=1.6, so x2=2.56x^2=2.56x2=2.56. No average over different observations is used here.
Per observation, log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qφ(z∣x)\log p(x,z)-\log q_\varphi(z\mid x)logp(x,z)−logqφ​(z∣x) is L=C−12Eq[(x−z)2+z2]+log⁡s\mathcal L=C-\tfrac12\mathbb E_q[(x-z)^2+z^2]+\log sL=C−21​Eq​[(x−z)2+z2]+logs, where C=(1−log⁡(2π))/2C=(1-\log(2\pi))/2C=(1−log(2π))/2.
Using the encoder mean and variance gives log⁡p(x,z)−log⁡qφ(z∣x)\log p(x,z)-\log q_\varphi(z\mid x)logp(x,z)−logqφ​(z∣x) for this fixed observation J(a,s)=C−1.28[(1−a)2+a2]−s2+log⁡sJ(a,s)=C-1.28[(1-a)^2+a^2]-s^2+\log sJ(a,s)=C−1.28[(1−a)2+a2]−s2+logs. Expand the two squares in the appendix.
Calculation ·

A correct centre does not guarantee a correct guess

Force the encoder standard deviation to remain s=1s=1s=1. It can match the posterior centre, but its variance is twice the true variance.
For matching Gaussian means, the divergence is 12[1/(1/2)−1+log⁡((1/2)/1)]=12(1−log⁡2)≈0.153\tfrac12[1/(1/2)-1+\log((1/2)/1)]=\tfrac12(1-\log2)\approx0.15321​[1/(1/2)−1+log((1/2)/1)]=21​(1−log2)≈0.153.
Even a separate best guess for each observation cannot fix that spread. This is an approximation gap, rather than an extra cost of sharing an encoder.
Supplement · Earlier coin examples and comparisons

Inference is a bill we pay again after every update

We already know how to infer a hidden cause for one observation.

Today: stop paying per record. Train one function that outputs the answer, once and for all.
SoRepeated observations repeat the same inference work.NextOur goal is to replace repeated inference with one reusable function.
Supplement · Earlier coin examples and comparisons

Two results from earlier lectures that return today

1. In the E-step of expectation–maximization , what is computed for each record?
Answer. The posterior over the hidden variable, recomputed for every record in every round. Returns in Part 1, as the work we want to stop repeating.
2. The evidence lower bound is a bound on what, and how large is the gap?
Answer. On log⁡p(x)\log p(x)logp(x), from below; the gap is the Kullback–Leibler divergence KL(q ∥ p(z∣x))\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(z\mid x))KL(q∥p(z∣x)). Returns in Part 3, as what we train the network to maximize.

An encoder maps an observation to a distribution

Our input is the head count; our output is a probability for coin A.

Definition. An encoder qφ(z∣x)q_\varphi(z\mid x)qφ​(z∣x) is a function with parameters φ\varphiφ that takes an observation xxx and returns a distribution over the hidden variable zzz. Ours is qφ(A∣h)=σ(a+b⋅h),φ=(a,b).q_\varphi(A\mid h)=\sigma(a+b\cdot h),\qquad \varphi=(a,b).qφ​(A∣h)=σ(a+b⋅h),φ=(a,b).

σ(t)=1/(1+e−t)\sigma(t)=1/(1+e^{-t})σ(t)=1/(1+e−t) turns a score into a probability; two parameters in all, shared by every observation

Two networks learn the guesses and the model

So far the coin probabilities were supplied; now let the generative model learn too.

Encoder: reads a bag's toss result xxx, then outputs a guess about its hidden coin zzz.

Decoder: takes a hidden choice zzz, then specifies probabilities for possible observations xxx.

Train both with the same bound. With neural networks, this is a variational autoencoder. The encoder outputs a distribution, not a known hidden answer.

SoTrain the encoder and decoder together using the lower bound.NextWe have met the two tasks of inferring hidden choices and updating the model before.

Both use the evidence lower bound. A shared encoder replaces separate posterior calculations.
